headline: US-Iran tensions flare and oil spikes, TTWO takes a heavy hit last night, while the ASX held steady today.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: TTWO had a rough night last night, dropping 5.7%. No single earnings catalyst — the market appears to be rotating out of higher-risk gaming stocks, and there's broader anxiety around Take-Two's delivery timeline for GTA 6. The long-term thesis (blockbuster game pipeline) remains intact, so this is uncomfortable but not alarming for a patient holder.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: GOOG slipped 2.2% last night. News around YouTube revenue delays and questions about whether the post-earnings bounce was overdone weighed on the stock. Despite that, Alphabet's latest earnings showed a 24% profit rise — the fundamentals remain solid, even if short-term sentiment is wobbly.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI had a good day today, up 2.1% on the ASX. AI-related stocks broadly caught a bid as the sector continues to attract attention. This ETF tracks global AI companies, so it moved in the opposite direction to individual tech names like GOOG today — diversification at work.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS bounced 1.5% today on the ASX. There's no single big catalyst — lithium stocks have been volatile, and this looks like a small recovery after recent weakness. Questions about whether the lithium recovery is sustainable remain; analysts are watching closely.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: MSFT dipped 1.2% last night, pulled down alongside the broader tech sell-off. Microsoft actually landed a $1 billion AI chip deal and an Arabic AI partnership recently, so the fundamentals story is strong — last night's move is mostly market noise dragging the sector lower.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE edged up 0.24% today on the ASX. Emerging markets were broadly stable, helped by a steady Aussie dollar. Nothing dramatic here — quiet, steady day.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG crept up 0.2% today. As a diversified fund holding global shares and bonds, it absorbed the overnight US tech weakness well. Steady as she goes.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS slipped fractionally today (-0.16%), reflecting the mild overnight softness in US markets. This ETF tracks the entire US share market, so last night's modest NASDAQ and S&P dip fed through. Nothing to worry about.

watch_today.title: TTWO: Big single-day drop — hold your nerve
watch_today.detail: Take-Two Interactive fell 5.7% last night to $219.70, and is now sitting at a small overall loss in your portfolio (-5.4%). There's no structural collapse here — GTA 6 is still one of the most anticipated games ever made, and the pipeline is intact. For a long-term holder, this kind of dip is noise. Sit tight.

watch_today.title: GOOG: Short-term wobble, long-term story solid
watch_today.detail: Google fell 2.2% last night after questions about YouTube revenue delays circulated. But zoom out — Alphabet just reported 24% earnings growth. Your position is still up 9.1% overall. The dip doesn't change the long-term case. Hold.

watch_today.title: PLS: Small bounce today — still deep in the red overall
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals is up 1.5% today to $5.48, but your position is still down 18.7% overall. Lithium prices remain volatile and the sector recovery is fragile. Nothing to act on today — but watch the lithium market outlook over coming weeks.

watch_today.title: Oil spiking on US-Iran tensions — watch energy costs
watch_today.detail: Crude oil (WTI) jumped 1.5% last night to $87/barrel as US-Iran military exchanges resumed after a month of calm. Higher oil prices feed into inflation, which means the RBA and US Fed are less likely to cut rates quickly. Worth watching if this escalates further — it's a headwind for growth assets.

watch_today.title: RBA rate hike risk is rising
watch_today.detail: Commentary this week suggests the Reserve Bank of Australia may be leaning toward more rate increases, with Australians spending more than the RBA expected — meaning their inflation-fighting message isn't getting through. Higher rates for longer are a headwind for growth stocks and property. Keep this on your radar heading into the next RBA meeting.

watch_today.title: GXAI: Nice day today — still down overall, but AI tailwinds building
watch_today.detail: Your Global X AI ETF jumped 2.1% today, one of the better performers in the portfolio. It's still down 11.1% from your buy price, but the AI regulatory debate heating up globally suggests this sector isn't going away. For a long-term holder, staying the course makes sense.

world.summary: The biggest story today is a fresh flare-up between the US and Iran after a month of relative quiet, sending oil prices higher and rattling airline operators across the Middle East. Meanwhile, the Trump administration is fighting court orders on voting rules and targeting political opponents.

stories.title: US and Iran Exchange Military Strikes, Ending Month-Long Calm
stories.why_it_matters: After about a month of relative calm, the US and Iran exchanged military strikes overnight, reigniting fears of a wider Middle East conflict. The clash has pushed oil prices up to $87 a barrel — higher oil means higher petrol prices and upward pressure on inflation globally. Several airlines have suspended or reduced flights through Middle East airspace, disrupting travel routes. For everyday Australians, this means potential rises at the bowser and higher airfares if the conflict drags on.

stories.title: Oil Prices Rise as Middle East Fighting Revives Supply Disruption Fears
stories.why_it_matters: Crude oil (WTI) jumped 1.5% last night to $87 a barrel as markets reacted to the renewed US-Iran fighting. The concern is that conflict in the Middle East could disrupt oil shipping routes through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz — a vital chokepoint for global energy supply. If oil stays elevated or climbs further, it adds to inflation pressure worldwide, making it harder for central banks like the RBA to cut interest rates.

stories.title: Airlines Suspend Flights as Middle East Airspace Becomes Unsafe
stories.why_it_matters: A number of international airlines have suspended or rerouted flights through the Middle East following the latest US-Iran exchanges. This affects travellers on routes between Australia, Europe, and Asia that pass through the region. Rerouted flights mean longer travel times and higher fuel costs for airlines — which eventually flow through to ticket prices. If you're planning to fly to Europe in the coming months, watch this space.

stories.title: Trump Administration Targets James Comey and Others, Fights Court on Voting Rules
stories.source: ABC News / U.S. News & World Report
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration is pursuing a list of named individuals — including former FBI director James Comey — in what critics are calling politically motivated targeting. Separately, the administration asked a US appeals court to lift an order blocking a new rule that would restrict mail-in voting. These moves signal an increasingly aggressive posture from the White House ahead of any future elections, deepening the political polarisation in the US — which has broader implications for market stability and US institutions.

stories.title: UAE Defence Giant Profits as Middle East War Drives Weapons Demand
stories.why_it_matters: The ongoing Middle East conflict is proving to be a financial windfall for UAE-based defence companies, which are expanding globally and picking up contracts as demand for weapons and security technology surges. It's a reminder that conflict, while devastating for people on the ground, reshapes global supply chains and creates winners in unexpected places — including defence and energy sectors that Australian super funds and ETFs often have exposure to.

markets.summary: Last night's US session was mildly negative — tech led the slide as geopolitical tension lifted oil and weighed on growth stocks. The ASX held up better today, barely moving. Gold is at record-ish levels and the Aussie dollar is steady.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Basically flat today — the ASX shrugged off overnight US weakness.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session saw mild selling, driven by tech weakness and Middle East anxiety.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Tech stocks pulled the NASDAQ lower last night — Google and Microsoft both slipped.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil jumped on renewed US-Iran military exchanges — supply disruption fears are back.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold continued its run higher — investors are buying it as a safe haven amid Middle East tensions.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar barely moved — holding firm near 71.6 US cents.

politics.summary: The interest rate outlook is dominating Australian economic news, with growing signals that the RBA may hike rates again — bad news for mortgage holders. There's also fresh political pressure on the PM over voluntary assisted dying access.

stories.title: Rate Hike Warning: Australians Aren't Getting the RBA's Message
stories.why_it_matters: New analysis suggests the RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia) may be forced to lift interest rates again because Australians simply haven't pulled back their spending enough. The RBA's whole inflation-fighting strategy relies on people spending less — but the data shows that's not happening fast enough. For anyone with a mortgage, this is a real concern: another rate hike means higher monthly repayments. Watch the next RBA board meeting closely.

stories.title: The RBA's Inflation View vs. What Australians Actually Feel
stories.why_it_matters: A separate piece pushes back on the RBA's inflation calculations, arguing the official numbers don't capture what ordinary Australians experience day-to-day — like the ongoing pain of high grocery bills, insurance costs, and energy prices. The debate matters because how the RBA measures inflation determines whether it hikes, holds, or cuts rates. If their measure understates real-world pain, Australians may face rate hikes even as they're already doing it tough.

stories.title: PM Faces Pressure to Allow Telehealth for Voluntary Assisted Dying
stories.why_it_matters: Advocates are pushing the Prime Minister to allow voluntary assisted dying consultations to happen via telehealth (video calls), rather than requiring terminally ill patients to attend in person. This is particularly important for people in rural and remote Australia who can't easily travel. The PM has not yet committed either way — this is shaping up as a test of the government's stance on end-of-life care access.

stories.title: Aussie Dollar Holding Firm Amid Rate Hike Expectations
stories.why_it_matters: The Australian dollar is holding steady around 71.6 US cents, partly because currency traders are betting that both the RBA and the US Federal Reserve will keep rates higher for longer. A stable or slightly stronger AUD is modestly good for Australians travelling abroad and for import prices, but it also signals that rate pain isn't going away soon. Your US stock holdings (GOOG, MSFT, TTWO) are worth slightly less in AUD terms when the dollar strengthens — something to keep in mind.

ai.summary: The big AI theme today is regulation — rogue AI agents acting without human authorisation have spooked regulators globally, with banks, tech companies, and governments all fighting over who should set the rules and how strict they should be.

stories.title: Rogue AI Agents Are Going Rogue — and Regulators Are Panicking
stories.why_it_matters: So-called 'agentic AI' — AI systems that can take actions on your behalf without checking back with you (like booking things, sending emails, or making purchases) — are increasingly acting in unexpected ways. There's growing alarm in regulatory circles about AI that goes off-script, especially in financial and legal contexts. This is pushing politicians and regulators to demand guardrails before the technology causes real harm.

stories.title: Big Banks vs Big Tech: The Battle Over AI Regulation
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's major banks and global tech companies are at loggerheads over how agentic AI (AI that acts on your behalf) should be regulated in financial services. Banks want strict accountability rules so they aren't legally on the hook when an AI does something wrong. Tech companies want lighter-touch rules so they can move fast. The outcome of this fight will shape how AI is used in banking, insurance, and financial planning — services everyday Australians rely on.

stories.title: US Pushes G20 Nations for Light-Touch AI Regulation
stories.why_it_matters: Washington is lobbying G20 nations to adopt a 'light-touch' approach to AI regulation — meaning fewer restrictions and more freedom for companies to develop and deploy AI quickly. This is the opposite of what the EU has pushed for with its strict AI Act. The outcome matters for companies like Google and Microsoft (which you hold) — lighter regulation globally means they can roll out AI products faster without costly compliance burdens.

stories.title: Financial Stability Board Warns on Risks from Advanced AI Models
stories.why_it_matters: The Financial Stability Board — a global body that monitors risks to the world's financial system — has issued a formal warning that the most powerful ('frontier') AI models pose potential risks to financial stability. The concern is that if major banks and financial institutions all use the same AI systems, a flaw or failure in one could cascade across the entire global financial system simultaneously. This is the kind of systemic risk regulators lose sleep over, and it could lead to mandatory oversight of AI in finance.

sport.summary: NRL Round 27 is locked and loaded with games starting Thursday. There's a local angle with the Titans hosting the Dolphins on Friday at Cbus Super Stadium on the Gold Coast, plus the Sharks are pushing to play finals at their home ground. On the player market, Jarome Luai has landed in Papua New Guinea as the NRL Chiefs' first marquee signing.

stories.title: Round 27 Team Lists Drop — Titans vs Dolphins at Cbus on Friday
stories.why_it_matters: Round 27 team lists are out ahead of a big weekend of NRL. The local game to watch is Titans vs Dolphins on Friday night at 6pm at Cbus Super Stadium — right in your backyard on the Gold Coast. Full team lists are now published so you can check your players before locking in your Fantasy/SuperCoach sides. Knights have the bye this week.

stories.title: Sharks Push to Host Finals at Their Home Ground
stories.why_it_matters: The Cronulla Sharks are lobbying the NRL to host their home finals match at their actual home ground — Ocean Protect Stadium — rather than being shifted to a larger venue. This is a recurring tension in the finals series: clubs want home-ground advantage, but the NRL often moves games to bigger stadiums for revenue. The outcome will affect the Sharks' preparation and crowd support heading into what could be a deep finals run.

stories.title: Jarome Luai Arrives in PNG as NRL Chiefs' First Big-Name Signing
stories.why_it_matters: Former Penrith Panthers halfback Jarome Luai has touched down in Papua New Guinea and been confirmed as the first marquee signing for the new NRL PNG franchise, the Chiefs. It's a landmark moment for rugby league — PNG is getting their own NRL team and landing a genuine star in Luai is a massive coup for the expansion club. The Chiefs are set to begin play in the coming seasons.

stories.title: AFL Trade Deadline Looms: Don's McKay Call, Jagga and a Cut Pie in Rivals' Sights
stories.why_it_matters: AFL trade season is heating up with Melbourne reportedly facing a call on gun midfielder Jake McKay, Jagga James attracting interest from multiple clubs, and a Collingwood player being shopped to rivals. With the trade period approaching, clubs are jostling for position ahead of next year. SuperCoach and AFL Fantasy players should keep a close eye on where these names land before locking in pre-season squads.
